subject: chemistry
prompt: A student heats one end of a metal wire. The other end gets hot quickly. Which two metals are the **best conductors of heat**?

image.alt: A metal wire clamped on a stand and heated at one end with a pin stuck on the far end with wax

hint: Think of what cooking vessels and heating coils are made from.
explanation: **Silver and copper** are the best conductors of heat. **Lead and mercury** are comparatively poor conductors, which is why they are the usual wrong choice. Metals in general conduct heat well and have high melting points, so the wire does not melt in the flame.

subject: chemistry
prompt: A pin is stuck with wax to the far end of a metal wire. The wire is heated. Tap the part that **shows the heat has travelled along the wire**.

image.alt: A heated metal wire with a pin stuck on its free end with wax

hint: Something falls off when the wax softens.
explanation: Heat conducted through the **wire** reaches the far end and melts the **wax**, so the **pin drops**. Only the end near the flame is heated directly, so the falling pin is the evidence of conduction (Activity 3.5).

subject: chemistry
prompt: Metals can be hammered into sheets and drawn into wires. Which of these are **general properties of metals**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A metal being hammered into a sheet and drawn into a wire

options.text: Shiny (lustrous) when the surface is clean
Can be beaten into thin sheets
Brittle, breaking into pieces when hammered
Good conductors of heat and electricity
Sonorous: produce a ringing sound when struck

hint: Metals are the opposite of brittle. Only one metal is a liquid.
explanation: Metals are lustrous, **malleable**, **ductile**, **sonorous** and good conductors of heat and electricity. Being brittle is a property of non-metals. Almost all metals are solids at room temperature; **mercury** is the only liquid metal (gallium and caesium merely melt easily).

subject: chemistry
prompt: About 2 km of gold wire can be drawn from 1 g of gold. How much wire could be drawn from **5 g** of gold?

image.alt: A metal drawn through a die into a thin wire

hint: Gold is the most ductile metal. More gold gives proportionally more wire.
explanation: Length is proportional to mass: $5 \times 2\ \text{km} = 10\ \text{km}$. The traps: dividing instead of multiplying ($2 \div 5$ is far too small, and $5 \div 2 = 2.5$ uses the wrong ratio) and adding ($2 + 5 = 7$) as if the masses were lengths.

subject: chemistry
prompt: You want to test whether a metal conducts electricity. You place it in the circuit between terminals A and B. Tap the **metal sample being tested**.

image.alt: A circuit with a battery, a bulb, a switch and a metal sample between terminals A and B

hint: It sits in the gap between A and B.
explanation: The sample completes the circuit between **A and B**. If it is a metal, current flows and the **bulb glows**. A non-metal such as sulphur would leave the bulb dark (graphite, an allotrope of carbon, is the exception).

subject: chemistry
prompt: Elements do not always follow the general rules for metals and non-metals. Match each element with its unusual property.

image.alt: Mercury, iodine, graphite and sodium

right.text: A metal that is a liquid at room temperature
A metal soft enough to cut with a knife

hint: Alkali metals are soft; one allotrope of carbon conducts.
explanation: **Mercury** is the only liquid metal. **Sodium** (like lithium and potassium) is so soft it can be cut with a knife. **Graphite**, an allotrope of carbon, conducts electricity. **Iodine** is a non-metal yet lustrous. This is why elements cannot be grouped by physical properties alone.

subject: chemistry
prompt: A copper wire is heated strongly in air. What happens?

image.alt: Magnesium, copper, iron filings and gold in a flame

options.text: It burns with a dazzling white flame
It does not burn but gets a black coating of copper(II) oxide
It catches fire without being heated
Nothing at all happens, as copper does not react with oxygen

hint: Compare the four samples: only one burns with a dazzling flame.
explanation: Copper does not burn, but the hot metal gets a **black layer of copper(II) oxide**: $\ce{2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO}$. The dazzling white flame belongs to magnesium. Only silver and gold show no reaction with oxygen even at high temperatures.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Aluminium oxide reacts with both hydrochloric acid (an acid) and sodium hydroxide (a base). Such oxides are called amphoteric oxides. Which pair are both **amphoteric oxides**?

image.alt: Aluminium oxide reacting with an acid on one side and a base on the other

hint: Amphoteric means it behaves as both a base and an acid.
explanation: Oxides that react with **both acids and bases** to give salt and water are **amphoteric**: $\ce{Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O}$ and $\ce{Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O}$. Zinc oxide behaves the same way. The other pairs are ordinary basic oxides.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Sodium under kerosene and sodium burning in open air

assertion: Sodium is stored under kerosene oil.
reason: In the open, sodium reacts so strongly with oxygen and moisture that it catches fire.
hint: Ask what would happen if sodium were left in the open.
explanation: Both statements are true and R explains A. **Sodium and potassium** are so reactive that they can catch fire in the open, so they are kept **immersed in kerosene oil** to cut them off from air and moisture and prevent accidental fires.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Which picture shows the **safe** way to store a piece of sodium metal?

image.alt: A jar of water with sodium reacting
Sodium burning on an open dish
A jar of dilute acid with sodium bubbling
A jar of kerosene oil with sodium resting at the bottom

hint: Sodium reacts with water, air and acids.
explanation: Sodium must be kept away from air, water and acids. Only the container of **kerosene oil** (D) does that: sodium does not react with it. In water (A) it reacts violently and the hydrogen catches fire; on an open dish (B) it burns; in dilute acid (C) it reacts even faster.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Sodium reacts with cold water: $\ce{2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2}$. Suppose **4 mol** of sodium react completely. How many moles of hydrogen gas are released?

image.alt: A piece of sodium racing on water with hydrogen burning above it

hint: Read the mole ratio from the balanced equation: Na to H₂.
explanation: The balanced equation shows $2\ \text{mol Na} \to 1\ \text{mol H}_2$, so $4\ \text{mol Na} \to 2\ \text{mol H}_2$. Traps: assuming a 1:1 ratio (4 mol), copying the 1 mol of $\text{H}_2$ straight from the equation without scaling it up (1 mol), or doubling instead of halving (8 mol).

subject: chemistry
prompt: Arrange these metals in **increasing order of reactivity with water**. Start from the one that does not react at all and end with the one that reacts most violently.

image.alt: Metals tested with cold water, hot water and steam

items.text: Calcium: reacts with cold water, floats on bubbles
Copper: no reaction even with steam

hint: Ask which needs steam, which needs hot water and which reacts in cold water.
explanation: Copper (like lead, silver and gold) does not react with water. **Iron** (and Al, Zn) react only with **steam**. **Magnesium** reacts with **hot** water. **Calcium** reacts with **cold** water, less violently, and floats as hydrogen bubbles stick to it. **Sodium** and potassium react so violently that the hydrogen burns.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Match each metal with how it reacts with water.

image.alt: Metals tested with cold water, hot water and steam

right.text: No reaction with cold water, reacts with hot water
Does not react with water at all

hint: Move down the reactivity series.
explanation: $\ce{2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2}$ is so exothermic the hydrogen burns. **Calcium** reacts less violently and floats because bubbles of $\ce{H2}$ stick to it. **Magnesium** needs hot water. **Iron**: $\ce{3Fe + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4 + 4H2}$ with steam only. **Copper** does not react with water.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Iron, aluminium and zinc react only with steam. In this set-up, tap **where the metal reacts with the steam**.

image.alt: A flask producing steam, a heated tube holding a metal and a gas jar collecting hydrogen

spots.label: Metal sample in the heated tube

hint: Look for the solid sitting in the middle of the heated tube.
explanation: Steam from the flask passes over the **heated metal** in the middle of the tube. There it forms the metal oxide and hydrogen, for example $\ce{3Fe + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4 + 4H2}$. The hydrogen is then collected over water in the gas jar.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Look at how fast the bubbles form. Then arrange these metals in **decreasing order of their reactivity with dilute hydrochloric acid**.

image.alt: Five test tubes of dilute acid with different metals and different amounts of bubbles

hint: Compare the bubbles in each tube. Copper gives none.
explanation: The rate of bubbles and the heat given out fall in the order $\text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Zn} > \text{Fe}$. **Copper** shows no bubbles and no temperature change, because it lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series and cannot displace hydrogen from dilute acids.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Which of these metals will give bubbles of **hydrogen** with dilute hydrochloric acid? Select all that apply.

image.alt: The reactivity series from potassium to gold, with hydrogen marked

hint: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series displace it from dilute acids.
explanation: Metal + dilute acid $\to$ salt + hydrogen works only for metals **above hydrogen** in the reactivity series: Mg, Zn and Fe. **Copper and silver** are below hydrogen, so no bubbles are seen.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Hydrogen gas is **not** evolved (given off) when most metals react with dilute nitric acid. Why?

image.alt: A metal in nitric acid with brown fumes rising

options.text: Nitric acid is too weak to react with metals
HNO₃ is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises the H₂ formed to water
Hydrogen is very soluble in nitric acid

hint: Nitric acid does a different job from HCl or H₂SO₄.
explanation: **HNO₃ is a strong oxidising agent.** It oxidises the hydrogen produced to water and is itself reduced to nitrogen oxides such as N₂O, NO or NO₂ (the brown fumes). Only magnesium and manganese give H₂ with very dilute HNO₃.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A copper wire in iron sulphate and an iron nail in copper sulphate

assertion: A copper wire placed in iron(II) sulphate solution displaces iron from it.
reason: Copper is less reactive than iron.
hint: Which way does displacement go?
explanation: A is **false** and R is **true**. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution. Copper is less reactive than iron, so the copper wire does nothing, while an iron nail in copper sulphate gets a brown copper coat and the blue solution fades.

subject: chemistry
prompt: An iron nail is placed in copper(II) sulphate solution for about 20 minutes. Which test tube shows what you would **observe**?

image.alt: Blue solution and a clean iron nail
Colourless solution with gas bubbles
Deep blue solution and a coated nail
Pale green solution and a nail with a brown coat

hint: Iron is more reactive than copper. Copper(II) sulphate is blue, iron(II) sulphate is pale green.
explanation: $\ce{Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu}$. Iron displaces copper, so the nail gets a **reddish-brown coat of copper** and the **blue colour fades to pale green** as iron(II) sulphate forms. Tube C has the coat but an unchanged blue solution, which cannot happen because copper ions are used up. A and B show no displacement or a wrong product (no gas forms).

subject: chemistry
prompt: Four metals A, B, C and D were added to four salt solutions. Use the table to arrange them in **decreasing order of reactivity**.

image.alt: A table of metals A to D added to solutions of zinc sulphate, iron sulphate, copper sulphate and silver nitrate

hint: The more salts a metal can displace, the higher it sits in the series.
explanation: A metal displaces another metal from its salt only if it is **more reactive**. **A** displaces all four (even zinc), **B** displaces only Cu and Ag, **C** displaces only Ag, **D** displaces none. So A > B > C > D. The reversed order D > C > B > A is the common slip of reading displacement as being displaced.

subject: chemistry
prompt: The **thermit reaction** uses a metal from this series to displace iron from iron(III) oxide. Tap that metal.

image.alt: The reactivity series from potassium to gold

hint: It is cheap, common, above iron in the series and its oxide is Al₂O₃.
explanation: $\ce{Fe2O3 + 2Al -> 2Fe + Al2O3 + heat}$. **Aluminium** sits above iron, so it displaces iron from its oxide. The reaction is so exothermic that molten iron forms, used to weld railway tracks. K and Ca are too violent to handle, while Cu and Au are less reactive than iron.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Sodium (2,8,1) reacts with chlorine (2,8,7). Look at the electron counts. Then tap the **chloride ion**.

image.alt: Sodium and chlorine atoms before the reaction and their ions after it

hint: A chloride ion has gained an electron, completing its octet.
explanation: Chlorine gains one electron to complete its outer shell, becoming **Cl⁻ (2,8,8)** with 17 protons and 18 electrons. The sodium atom loses its single outer electron to become **Na⁺ (2,8)**. Neither ion should be confused with the neutral atoms on the left.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Put the steps in the formation of sodium chloride in the correct order.

image.alt: Sodium and chlorine atoms and the ions they form

items.text: A chlorine atom (2,8,7) gains that electron
Oppositely charged ions are held together by electrostatic attraction
A sodium atom (2,8,1) loses one electron
A sodium ion Na⁺ (2,8) with a stable octet forms

hint: Electrons must be lost before they can be gained.
explanation: Sodium loses its outer electron to reach the stable octet of the L shell, forming **Na⁺**. Chlorine takes up that electron to complete its octet, forming **Cl⁻**. The opposite charges attract strongly, giving the ionic compound NaCl, which exists as aggregates of ions rather than molecules.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Each atom below is drawn with its protons and electrons. Match each atom with the stable **ion** it forms.

image.alt: Bohr diagram of an atom with 11 protons
Bohr diagram of an atom with 17 protons
Bohr diagram of an atom with 8 protons
Bohr diagram of an atom with 12 protons

hint: Metals lose electrons, non-metals gain them, until the outer shell is complete.
explanation: **Na** (2,8,1) loses 1 electron: Na⁺. **Cl** (2,8,7) gains 1: Cl⁻. **O** (2,6) gains 2 to reach 2,8: O²⁻. **Mg** (2,8,2) loses 2: Mg²⁺. Every ion ends with a full outer shell like a noble gas.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Magnesium (atomic number 12) forms an ion in magnesium chloride. Which diagram shows the **magnesium ion** in $\ce{MgCl2}$?

image.alt: 12 protons and 12 electrons (2,8,2)
12 protons and 10 electrons (2,8)
12 protons and 11 electrons (2,8,1)
12 protons and 13 electrons (2,8,3)

hint: Metals form cations by losing electrons. How many does Mg need to lose to reach a full shell?
explanation: $\ce{Mg -> Mg^2+ + 2e-}$. The atom (2,8,2) loses its two outer electrons, leaving 12 protons and **10 electrons (2,8)**: a charge of $+2$. A is the neutral atom, C has lost only one electron (Mg⁺), and D has gained one, which a metal does not do. Each $\ce{Cl-}$ takes one electron, so two chloride ions are needed.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Which statements about ionic compounds such as sodium chloride are **correct**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A rigid lattice of positive and negative ions with a layer sliding

options.text: They have high melting and boiling points
They conduct electricity in the solid state
They dissolve easily in kerosene and petrol
They are brittle and break when pressure is applied
They are generally soluble in water

hint: A lot of energy is needed to break the attraction between ions, and ions can't move in a solid.
explanation: Strong electrostatic forces make ionic solids **hard, brittle** and give them **high melting and boiling points**. They dissolve in **water** but not in kerosene or petrol. They conduct only when the ions are free to move: **molten or dissolved**, not as a rigid solid. Sliding a layer puts like charges together, which is why the crystal breaks.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Sodium chloride as a solid, in water and molten, each in a bulb circuit

assertion: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does.
reason: Ionic compounds have high melting points.
hint: Why can the ions not carry current in the solid?
explanation: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. In the solid the ions are locked in a **rigid lattice**, so they cannot move. On melting, the heat overcomes the electrostatic attraction and the **ions move freely** to carry current. A high melting point is simply a separate property.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Sulphur is burnt, and the gas is collected in an inverted (upside-down) test tube. The gas is tested with **dry and moist blue litmus paper**. What happens?

image.alt: Sulphur burning under a test tube and dry and moist litmus strips

options.text: Dry litmus turns red, moist litmus stays blue
Dry litmus stays blue, moist litmus turns red

hint: The acid forms only when the gas meets water.
explanation: $\ce{S + O2 -> SO2}$. Sulphur dioxide has no action on **dry** litmus, but with moisture it forms sulphurous acid, $\ce{SO2 + H2O -> H2SO3}$, which turns **blue litmus red**. Most non-metals form acidic (or neutral) oxides, whereas metals form basic oxides.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Diamond and graphite, two forms of carbon

reason: Diamond is another allotrope (form) of carbon. It also conducts electricity.
hint: Check each allotrope separately.
explanation: A is **true** and R is **false**. Graphite conducts electricity, but **diamond**, the hardest natural substance, does not. Different forms of the same element (allotropes) can have very different properties; graphite is an exception among non-metals.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Ores mined from the earth are mixed with soil, sand and other impurities. What is this unwanted material called?

image.alt: An ore lump separated into soil and sand and the metal compound

hint: It is removed during the enrichment of the ore.
explanation: A **mineral** is any element or compound occurring naturally in the earth's crust. An **ore** is a mineral rich enough in a metal for profitable extraction. The impurities of soil and sand are called **gangue**, and they are removed before the metal is extracted.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Put the stages of getting a pure metal from nature in the correct order.

image.alt: An ore lump being separated into impurities and the metal compound

items.text: Mining the ore from the earth's crust

hint: You cannot refine a metal before you have extracted it.
explanation: Ores are first **mined**, then **enriched** to remove gangue, then the metal is **extracted** by a method chosen from its place in the reactivity series, and finally the impure metal is **refined**, most commonly electrolytically.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Tap the step in which **gangue** (soil, sand and other impurities) is removed from the ore.

image.alt: Four steps from ore to pure metal drawn as pictures

spots.label: Step 2: enrichment of the ore (gangue removed)

hint: The grains falling through the sieve are the impurities.
explanation: Mined ore is contaminated with **gangue**. It is removed in the **enrichment** step using differences in the physical or chemical properties of the ore and gangue. The furnace is the reduction step and the tank with electrodes is refining.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Which of these metals are found in nature in the **free (native) state**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: The reactivity series from potassium to gold

hint: Very unreactive metals sit at the bottom of the series.
explanation: Metals at the bottom of the series (gold, silver, platinum and copper) are so unreactive that they occur **free**. Sodium and calcium sit at the top: they are so reactive that they are **never found as free elements**.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Carbon cannot be used to get sodium from sodium oxide. Why?

image.alt: Metals in the activity series grouped by how they are extracted

options.text: Carbon is less dense than sodium
Carbon is a non-metal so it cannot react with oxides
Sodium has more affinity for oxygen than carbon has

hint: Reduction by carbon works only if carbon holds oxygen more strongly than the metal does.
explanation: Reduction by carbon works only if carbon has **more affinity for oxygen** than the metal. Metals high in the series (Na, K, Ca, Mg, Al) hold oxygen too strongly, so their oxides are reduced by **electrolysis** of the molten compound. Zn, Fe and Pb oxides can be reduced with carbon.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Which of these describes **calcination**?

image.alt: Two furnaces: a sulphide ore heated with lots of air and a carbonate ore with little air

options.text: Heating a sulphide ore strongly in excess air
Heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air
Heating a metal oxide with carbon
Passing electricity through a molten ore

hint: Compare the air supply and the gas produced in the two furnaces.
explanation: **Calcination**: carbonate ore heated strongly in limited air, e.g. $\ce{ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2}$. **Roasting** is for sulphide ores in excess air, e.g. $\ce{2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2}$. Oxides are easier to reduce than sulphides or carbonates, which is why both are converted to oxides first.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Mercury is obtained from its ore cinnabar (HgS). Put the steps in the correct order.

image.alt: Metals in the activity series grouped by how they are extracted

items.text: Mercury(II) oxide (HgO) and sulphur dioxide form
Liquid mercury and oxygen are obtained

hint: Mercury is low in the series, so heat alone is enough.
explanation: $\ce{2HgS + 3O2 ->[heat] 2HgO + 2SO2}$, then $\ce{2HgO ->[heat] 2Hg + O2}$. Mercury is very unreactive, so its oxide is reduced to the metal by **heating alone**, with no carbon needed.

subject: chemistry
prompt: In the thermit reaction $\ce{Fe2O3 + 2Al -> 2Fe + Al2O3 + heat}$, which substance is the **reducing agent** (the one that is oxidised)?

image.alt: Molten iron from the thermit reaction being poured between two railway tracks

hint: The reducing agent takes the oxygen away.
explanation: Aluminium takes oxygen from $\ce{Fe2O3}$, so it is **oxidised** and acts as the **reducing agent**. $\ce{Fe2O3}$ loses oxygen and is **reduced**. Fe and $\ce{Al2O3}$ are products. The heat is so great that the iron forms molten and can weld rail tracks.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Tap the vessel where **aluminium reduces iron(III) oxide** to produce molten iron.

image.alt: Molten iron from a crucible poured into the gap between two railway tracks

hint: The reaction happens before the iron pours out.
explanation: The mixture of Fe₂O₃ and Al reacts in the **crucible**, releasing so much heat that iron forms in the molten state. The molten iron then flows into the gap and joins the two rail pieces.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Molten (melted) sodium chloride is electrolysed. What is **deposited at the cathode**?

image.alt: Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride

hint: Positive ions move to the negative electrode.
explanation: Metals high in the series are obtained by electrolysis of their molten chlorides. At the cathode: $\ce{Na+ + e- -> Na}$. At the anode: $\ce{2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-}$. So sodium is deposited at the **cathode** and chlorine is released at the **anode**. Hydrogen could appear only if water were present.

subject: chemistry
prompt: In the **electrolytic refining of copper**, tap the electrode that is made of **impure copper**.

image.alt: Electrolytic refining of copper with an impure copper electrode and a thin pure copper strip

spots.label: Cathode: thin strip of pure copper

hint: The impure metal dissolves; pure metal grows on the other electrode.
explanation: The **impure copper is the anode**. It dissolves into the acidified copper sulphate solution while an equal amount of **pure copper is deposited on the cathode**, a thin strip of pure copper. Insoluble impurities settle below the anode as **anode mud**.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Match each process with what it involves.

image.alt: Two furnaces heating a sulphide ore with plenty of air and a carbonate ore with little air

right.text: Sulphide ore heated strongly in excess air
Carbonate ore heated strongly in limited air
Aluminium reduces iron(III) oxide to molten iron
Impure metal as anode, pure metal deposited on cathode

hint: Roasting uses plenty of air, calcination limited air.
explanation: **Roasting** turns sulphides into oxides (SO₂ is released). **Calcination** turns carbonates into oxides (CO₂ is released). The **thermit reaction** welds railway tracks. **Electrolytic refining** is the most widely used way of purifying metals such as copper, zinc, tin, nickel, silver and gold.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Iron nails are left in three test tubes for a few days. Tap the substance in tube C that **absorbs moisture** from the air.

image.alt: Three test tubes A, B and C each holding an iron nail

spots.label: Rusting nail in water with air (tube A)
Layer of oil that keeps out air (tube B)
Anhydrous calcium chloride (drying agent, tube C)

hint: It is the white powder at the bottom of the dry tube.
explanation: **Anhydrous calcium chloride** soaks up moisture, so the nail in tube C meets only dry air and does not rust. Only tube A, with both air and water, shows rust. The oil on boiled water in tube B stops air reaching the nail. Iron rusts only when **both air (oxygen) and water** are present.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Which of these are ways of **preventing the rusting of iron**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Test tubes showing the conditions needed for iron to rust

options.text: Making an alloy such as stainless steel

hint: Rusting needs air and water. Block them or change the metal.
explanation: Rusting is prevented by **painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising, chrome plating, anodising or alloying**. Leaving iron in moist air or salt water speeds up rusting. Stainless steel (iron with nickel and chromium) is hard and does not rust.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A zinc-coated iron sheet with a scratch showing iron underneath

assertion: A galvanised iron article is protected from rusting even if the zinc coating is scratched.
reason: Zinc is more reactive than iron. So it is used up first and protects the iron.
hint: Which of the two metals loses electrons more easily?
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Zinc is **more reactive** than iron, so even when the coating is broken, the zinc corrodes in preference to the iron. This is why **galvanisation** (coating with a thin layer of zinc) protects iron and steel.

subject: chemistry
prompt: An alloy is a **homogeneous mixture** (a mixture that is the same throughout) of a metal with one or more other elements. Which diagram shows an alloy?

image.alt: Two kinds of atom mixed evenly
Two kinds of atom in two separate layers
Atoms of one kind in a regular pattern
Atoms of two kinds spread far apart

hint: Homogeneous means the same throughout, with more than one element.
explanation: In an alloy, atoms of the added element are **mixed evenly** with the main metal, as in diagram A. B is two separate layers (not mixed), C is a pure metal, and D shows widely separated atoms, as in a gas. Alloys are made by melting the primary metal and dissolving the other elements in it in definite proportions.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Match each alloy with its composition.

image.alt: Atoms of a pure metal compared with atoms of an alloy

right.text: An alloy in which one metal is mercury

hint: Solder is used for joining wires: it has a low melting point.
explanation: **Brass**: Cu + Zn. **Bronze**: Cu + Sn. **Solder**: Pb + Sn, with a low melting point for joining electrical wires. An **amalgam** contains mercury. Alloys usually conduct electricity less well and melt at lower temperatures than the pure metals.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Gold used for jewellery in India is generally **22 carat**. This means 22 parts of pure gold are alloyed (mixed) with 2 parts of copper or silver. What percentage of the alloy is gold?

image.alt: A circle of 24 equal parts of which 22 are gold

hint: Pure gold is 24 carat, so compare 22 with the total.
explanation: Total parts $= 22 + 2 = 24$, so gold $= \dfrac{22}{24} \times 100 = 91.7\%$. Traps: reading 22 as a percentage (22 %), using the copper share ($\frac{2}{24} = 8.3\%$), and subtracting 2 carats twice (83.3 %). Pure gold (24 carat) is too soft, so it is alloyed to harden it.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Tarnished copper vessels (vessels that have lost their shine) are cleaned with lemon or tamarind juice. Why does this work?

image.alt: A tarnished green copper pot cleaned with lemon juice becomes shiny

options.text: The juice adds a shiny layer of tin
The acid in the juice reacts with the basic copper carbonate coating and removes it
The juice is a strong base that dissolves copper
The juice reduces copper to a softer metal

hint: Acids neutralise bases. What is the green layer?
explanation: The green coat is **basic copper carbonate**, formed when copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide in air. Sour substances contain **acids** that react with and dissolve this basic coating, revealing bright copper again.

subject: chemistry
prompt: A man dipped gold bangles in a solution. They became shiny but lost a lot of their weight. Which solution did he most likely use?

image.alt: Two acids poured into a beaker where a gold ring is dissolving

options.text: A freshly prepared 3 : 1 mixture of concentrated HCl and concentrated HNO₃

hint: Gold dissolves only in a special mixture of two acids.
explanation: **Aqua regia** ('royal water') is a freshly prepared 3 : 1 mixture of concentrated HCl and concentrated HNO₃. It can dissolve gold and platinum, though neither acid can do so alone. The dissolving gold made the bangles lose weight.

subject: chemistry
prompt: Aluminium is a highly reactive metal. Still, it is used to make cooking utensils. Why?

image.alt: Anodising bath and a thin and a thicker oxide layer on aluminium

options.text: It is covered with a thin, protective layer of aluminium oxide
It does not react with oxygen

It is a poor conductor of heat

hint: What forms on the surface when aluminium meets air?
explanation: Aluminium forms a thin, tough layer of **aluminium oxide** in air, which prevents further oxidation. **Anodising** thickens this layer so aluminium resists corrosion even better. Aluminium actually conducts heat well, which is another reason it is used for utensils.
